div.p: While utilization bound based schedulability test is simple and effective, it is often difficult to derive the bound itself. For its analytical complexity, utilization bound results are usually obtained on a case-by-case basis. In this paper, we develop a general framework that allows one to effectively derive schedulability bounds for a wide range of real-time systems with different workload patterns and schedulers. Our analytical model is capable of describing a wide range of tasks and schedulers' behaviors. We propose a new definition of utilization, called workload rate. While similar to utilization, workload rate enables flexible representation of different scheduling and workload scenarios and leads to uniform derivation of schedulability bounds. We derive a parameterized schedulability bound for static priority schedulers with arbitrary priority assignment. Existing utilization bounds for different priority assignments and task releasing patterns can be derived from our closedform formula by simple assignments of proper parameters.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Meeting timing requirements is critical to many computer applications. These real-time systems are usually equipped with schedulability test, which determines whether each of the admitted tasks can meet its deadline. A new task will not be admitted unless it passes the schedulability test. The schedulability test can be either direct or indirect. Direct schedulability test will calculate the worst-case delays of the tasks in order to determine the permissibility of a new task. This type of test is accurate, but the computing cost in calculating the delays is very high.

The utilization based test is the most common indirect schedulability test which does not compute the delays, but tests system resource utilization to determine the task schedulability. A new task can be admitted only if the utilization is lower than a pre-derived bound. Utilization based test is extremely efficient with an on-line computing complexity of O (1).

Various utilization bounds have been derived in literature, and many have been implemented in mission critical systems. Some of the most notable results include 69% (and extensions) for the Rate/Deadline Monotonic scheduler (RMS/DMS) [26], [31], [35], [36], and [41]; 100% for Earliest Deadline First scheduler (EDF) [31]; and 33% for the Timed Token protocol (TTP) [3], [34], [48], and [49]; etc. Utilization bounds of RMS/DMS in multiprocessor systems are derived in [6], [7], [8], [9], [20], and [37]. Some utilization bounds for non-periodic systems are derived in [1], [2], and [47]. A more detailed summary of the literature is given in the next section.
In general, it is difficult to generalize the utilization bound method to non-periodic system due to the following two problems: a) Ambiguity in defining utilization for non-periodic tasks.

Utilization is a measurement of the resource consumption rate within a certain window of time (referred to as a measuring window). Typically, for periodic systems, task periods have been used as the length of measuring window. It is difficult to extend this definition to the domain of non-periodic tasks because one cannot have a well-defined notion of "period". b) Ad hoc-ness in the derivation of the utilization bound.
Most utilization bound results are obtained case-bycase, and the method developed for one system cannot be easily applied to another.

In this paper, we introduce an analytical model that is capable of describing a wide range of tasks and schedulers' behaviors. In addition to addressing the problems mentioned above, we broaden the utilization bound derivation techniques using the following approach:

• We propose a new definition of utilization, called workload rate, which measures the resource demand within a time window of length proportional to the deadline of a task, so that it can be used to characterize the demand of both periodic and non-periodic tasks in the same framework. • On the basis of the network calculus framework [40], [11]- [14], and [16]- [18], we derive key relationships between workload and services, to arrive at a lower bound of workload rate for arbitrary workload patterns and schedulers. • We derive a closed-form, parameterized workload rate bound for static priority systems. We show that the existing bounds are points and curves of our new bounds in a three dimensional space. Not only does our bound verify existing results, but it also reveals new results that has not been obtained otherwise. Our bound is directly reduced to the utilization bounds of the following platforms: o RMS system with periodic tasks whose deadlines are equal to periods [31]. o RMS system with periodic tasks whose deadlines are less than periods [26] and [41]. o RMS system with periodic tasks whose deadlines are multiples of periods [25]. o RMS system with multiframe tasks whose deadlines are equal to periods [36]. To our best knowledge, no current literature covers as wide a range of systems as our bound result.
• The parameterized bound for static priority scheduler with arbitrary priority assignment is further improved based on the concept of harmonic chain tasks [15] and [22].

div.head: Related work
div.p: In their seminal work [31], the authors derived the well-known 69% utilization bound for the RMS on single processor systems, where relative deadlines of periodic tasks are equal to their periods. This result has been extended to arbitrary deadline assignment schemes in [25], [26] and [41]. In [23] and [29], the authors improved the bound by exploiting the ratio between the longest and shortest task periods. The work in [15] and [22] further improved the bound result with the concept of the harmonic chain that exploits the divisibility between periods. The authors in [21] introduced an algorithm that transforms the periodic task into a harmonic task set, which has a utilization bound of 1, and proved that the algorithm performs better than the bound derived in [29] and [31], at the cost of higher complexity.

Utilization bounds of static priority schedulers on the time token protocol in FDDI networks were derived in [3], [34], [48], and [49]. The utilization bound for static priority schedulers in a networked environment have been studied in [47]. Utilization bounds for non-periodic tasks have been addressed in [1], [2], and [33]. Utilization bounds for RMS/DMS in multi-processor systems have been studied in [6], [7], [8], [20], and [33].

Generalizing the definition of utilization from periodic tasks to aperiodic tasks has been studied in [1], [2], [6], [35], and [47]. In deriving the utilization bound for RMS with multiframe and general real-time task models, the authors in [35] and [36] proposed a maximum average utilization that allows calculation of utilization in an infinite measuring window. In the analysis of the utilization bound in a multi-node network environment with leaky bucket packet sources, the authors in [47] used a utilization definition that is based on the sustainable rate in the leaky bucket function. To derive the utilization bound for non-periodic tasks and multiprocessor systems, the authors in [1], [2], and [6] proposed a utilization definition that is based on relative deadlines of tasks, instead of periods.

The linear programming method that has been proposed for finding utilization bounds when task parameters are known a priori has been studied in [15], [24], and [38]. The work in [10] introduced a new schedulability test which is similar to utilization based admission control. Specifically they proved that for periodic tasks with RMS, a task set is schedulable if ( 1) 2 i u Π + ≤ , where u i is the utilization of the i th task.

Generalization of a periodic task model was proposed in [34] and [35], in which the authors derived a bound result for multiframe tasks which allows jobs in the same task to have different size, provided that the relative deadline is same as period length.

Using workload constraint function to model tasks can be traced back to [16], [17], i.e. leaky bucket constraints of network traffic. This concept was expanded in [47] to analyze the utilization bounds of static priority schedulers. The general model for real-time tasks proposed in [35] shares a similar concept, and it corresponds to a special group of workload constraint functions in multiframe forms. The idea of modeling schedulers with service constraint functions originated in [12], [13], [14], [18], and [39]. Workload constraint and service constraint functions have been used for direct schedulability test in [11], [18], [19], [42], and [43] among many others, but none of them is used for utilization based test. A comprehensive survey on task models is given in [44] The rest of the paper is organized as follows. The related work is discussed in Section 2. Section 3 introduces the system model. In Section 4, schedulability bounds are discussed and a general bound for arbitrary scheduler and tasks are derived. Section 5 derives a closed-form bound for RMS with a special type of task set. In section 6, the closed-form bound for RMS is generalized to arbitrary static priority schedulers and is further improved for the harmonic chain tasks. Conclusions and discussions are given in Section 7.

div.head: Schedulability bound for RMS
div.p: In this section, we will first introduce a special type of workload constraint function to represent a wide range of task workload. Then we will derive the service constraint functions for RMS based on Theorem 2. Specific workload and service constraint functions will then be plugged into Theorem 3 to obtain a parameterized, closedform schedulability bound for RMS. The closed-form bound result reduces to existing bounds when parameters are properly set.

div.head: Non-preemptive systems
div.p: In a non-preemptive system, a high priority task T i can be blocked by a lower priority task T j , j > i, for a length of J max , the maximum job size of T j . Thus, this nonpreemption effect will lead to a priority inversion for the length of J max . During this interval, the system acts as if T j has a higher priority than T i . div.head: Final remarks
div.p: Most bounds reported in earlier works were obtained by searching along the boundary between the spaces of schedulable and non-schedulable task sets. This approach is hurdled by the difficulty of finding an effective analytical representation of the boundary. To overcome this challenge, in this paper we follow the network calculus framework to derive a general schedulability bound by solving a minimization problem over the entire task set population.

We have derived closed-form, parameterized bounds for schedulability bound of arbitrary static priority scheduling systems. We show that existing bounds, e.g. [25], [26], [31], [35], [36], and [41] are simple points and curves of our bounds in three dimensional spaces.

The work reported in this paper can be extended in many different ways. This paper focuses on an infinite number of task sets and derives the worst-case schedulability bound. In practical systems, it is common that the task set is finite and some parameters are known beforehand. The schedulability bound can be further improved with linear programming methods [15], [24], and [38] or other techniques, e.g. periods transformation [21]. It can also be extended to parallel and distributed systems.
